title: Is it smart to get an investment property?
content: Buying a rental property and becoming a landlord may be a good investment … or not. But either way, it’s a job. In this week’s Ask the Expert, which is part of CNN’s Savings Challenge, Douglas Boneparth, certified financial planner and founder of Bone Fide Wealth, offers a few questions to gauge whether the move would be right for you. Reader: Is an investment property worth it? DOUG: The honest answer? It depends! And anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Investment properties can absolutely build wealth over time. The combination of rental income, appreciation and tax advantages like depreciation has made real estate a meaningful part of a lot of people’s financial lives. I get why it’s appealing. But here’s what the highlight reels on social media tend to leave out. Owning rental property is a job. You are a landlord. That means tenants, vacancies, maintenance calls, repairs you didn’t budget for and the occasional nightmare scenario that no spreadsheet prepares you for. Before you pull the trigger, I’d want you to honestly answer a few questions. If the numbers work and you have the stomach for it, real estate can be a legitimate wealth-building tool. If you’re stretching to make it work on paper, it’s probably not worth it. Run the numbers (not just the optimistic ones) and let those be your guide. Credit scores help determine if you get approved for a loan – or an insurance policy . The higher your score, the lower your interest rate and monthly payments. Many factors go into a score, but one way to raise yours quickly is to lower the utilization rate on your credit cards. That’s the percentage your outstanding balances together represent relative to your combined credit limit. For example, if you have a combined limit of $30,000 across three credit cards and your balances add up to $15,000, your utilization rate is 50%. title: ‘Separating wants and needs’: Milwaukee couple reconsider their financial habits
content: Being able to clear their credit card debts thanks to a modest inheritance was a gift for Mariza and Geffrey Gordon. And it boosted their credit scores by more than 100 points to roughly 750. But that alone will not remedy their financial situation of living paycheck to paycheck and not having enough saved for emergencies. A more permanent fix will involve changing their money habits. Their Savings Challenge work with financial educator Tiffany Aliche has shown the Milwaukee-based couple some things they weren’t willing to look at previously. “The most difficult thing and probably one of the better things was it (forced us) to face (our) financial habits, bad, good or indifferent,” Geffrey said. “A lot of times in the past we’ve avoided facing our habits …. And this is something I can take moving forward, to just be willing to face it. There’s no way to improve if you don’t face it.” But improving may be a bumpy ride for the foreseeable future. On the one hand, the couple has started to regularly consider what is necessary to spend money on versus what they’d like to spend money on. “Separating wants and needs will be helpful for us moving forward,” Geffrey said. For example, they have cut back on spending for clothes, travel, concerts and sporting events, he said. And while they bought a garbage disposal to replace their broken one, he noted, they decided not to install it since it would have cost them money and they realized they can live without it for now. But they did go ahead with two other big home expenses. They installed new carpeting because the old carpet had a terrible smell even after cleaning it, Mariza explained. And they bought some furniture for their bedroom, which had been bare except for the bed itself, she said. They put down $400 cash for the furniture and put the rest on a 0% store card, which they qualified for after their credit scores jumped. Mariza said they are paying off the purchase monthly, noting that they expect to clear that debt well before their 0% rate expires. Tiffany said she would have advised that they not take on any debt unless it secures safety and health for them. Mariza, who was laid off earlier this year from a job as a plan consultant at a financial services firm, hasn’t found a new position yet. Until she does, Tiffany told the couple to worry less about putting money away, and instead maintain the savings they have. But they said they are dipping into what remains of their inheritance and into the 20% of savings automatically set aside from Geffrey’s paycheck to pay Mariza’s $555 monthly car note and help cover general expenses. Still, Geffrey said he is glad he arranged for a direct deposit from his paycheck into savings, a setup that he expects to be more beneficial once his wife gets a job and they have two incomes again. At that point, he added, they plan to follow Tiffany’s advice to prioritize saving for emergencies. Their goal is having an emergency fund to cover them for six months in case either one loses a job again. At this writing, Mariza said she has been going on interviews and did freelance work curating an art show featuring local artists. As for health insurance, she said she is resigned to not having it for now and plans to sign onto her husband’s plan for 2027 if she doesn’t have a job by then. In the meantime, to save on food and other goods, the couple said they will continue buying in bulk at Costco and plan to cook more meals at home. Throughout their Savings Challenge, which coincided with Mariza’s layoff, she said she has learned to be more mindful of her blessings and not take them for granted, especially when she feels discouraged on the job front. “Things could be so much worse,” she said.
